Willem Einthoven. The Dutch physiologist who invented the string galvanometer and founded electrocardiography, transforming the study of the heart from physical examination alone to instrumental objectivity.

In 1903, Einthoven invented the string galvanometer, a sensitive detector of minute electrical currents that visualized the heart's electrical activity as deflections of a vibrating string. He used this apparatus to record the first human electrocardiograms, establishing characteristic waveforms for normal rhythm and identifying arrhythmias, ischaemia, and hypertrophy. His technique was non-invasive and immediately reproducible, which made it revolutionary for clinical practice.

Einthoven standardized the Einthoven triangle, the geometric framework for interpreting electrical vectors of the heart from three limb leads. He named the distinctive waves of the electrocardiogram as P, QRS, and T, names still in use more than a century later. He spent his entire career at the University of Leiden, where he refined and taught electrocardiographic method to generations of students.

His work represented a fundamental shift in medicine toward objective, measurable methods at the bedside. In 1924, Einthoven won the Nobel Prize for this innovation. The electrocardiogram remains the EKG in modern usage, the abbreviation derived from his German name, Elektrokardiogramm. His peers, like Ivan Pavlov and Karl Landsteiner, were also pioneering the measurement and systematization of living systems, each bringing new instruments and methods to reveal the hidden mechanisms of disease.
